utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: An unexpected pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: We aim to please. I'm -- if -- with your permission going to open this case on behalf of Mr. Bala. Then Mr. Bala himself will address the Court from his seat and we will then start calling the list of witnesses that has been presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you would like the Chamber's permission for a statement to be made by your client in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: We would indeed, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Under Rule 84 bis probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Counsel for the Prosecution, my colleagues for the Defence, Mr. Limaj, Mr. Musliu, Mr. Haradin Bala. I consider it an honour to open this case on behalf of Haradin Bala. I'm going to provide a brief outline of the witnesses who we propose to call. I shall refer, I hope also briefly, to certain principles of international law, but I'd like to start, if I may, with a few words about the context in which we are all here today, that is the context of an evolving and developing international criminal jurisprudence, the context of a 60-year experiment in creating an international rule of law to be applied to individual human beings as well as to governments and their agents. In 1948, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights said in the preamble: "Whereas it is essential if man is not to be compelled to have recourse as a last resort to rebellion against tyranny and oppression, that human rights should be protected by the rule of law..." I'm just reminding myself to slow down by putting on my French earphones. Half a century later in 1998, after long and bitter years of tyranny and oppression and as the MUP and the JNA closed in murderously on the people of Kosovo, Haradin Bala felt compelled, as a last resort in those words of the Universal Declaration, to take up his rifle, to leave his poor family compound in Korretice e Eperme, where he and others could hear already the distant fighting in Lapusnik. They knew that if ordinary people like them did not take a stand, then they and their families would lose their land, their homes, their livestock, and most probably their lives. Going back to the stated aims of the Universal Declaration. Article 11 proclaimed: "Everyone charged with a penal offence shall have the right to be presumed innocent according to law in a public trial at which he has all the guarantees necessary for his defence." That article was interpreted further by Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. And that covenant was passed, it was placed on -- open for signature in 1966. And if you permit me a moment of personal reflection, I went up to university in 1967, a few months after that covenant was published, 10 years before it was to gain the 35 ratifications that would be necessary for it to enter into force. And I well remember my colleagues in that international law club speaking dismissively of the international covenants: "No country will ever abide by them. You'll never have an international body that can police them. No state will ever permit some international court to have jurisdiction over its citizens." Notwithstanding the cynicism of my fellow students, I believed then, as I do now, that the Universal Declaration and the International Covenants are among the most important human statements ever written. And for most of the 30 or more years that I've been practicing law, I have found myself citing those covenants at conferences, in United Nations committees, in articles, to students, and before often rather perplexed judges, particularly in the United States. The right to be presumed innocent. It's a fine, it's a noble phrase. What is its weight in this courtroom? As I stand here today before a Tribunal that is striving to become the embodiment of that same principle of international law, I have great hope. I also have great concern. Most of us who normally practice in the common-law jurisdictions regard the jury as the most important safeguard of the principle that everyone should be presumed innocent. We generally find that juries take the business of sitting in judgement over a fellow human being with extreme seriousness. In the words of the Bible, "With that judgement wherewith ye judge, therewith shall ye be judged also." And juries get that. But we are learning here, too, as common-law people, that there are other safeguards in other systems from which we can learn. We have no parallel to the examining magistrate, the juge d'instruction. We don't have a career judiciary trained from law school for that very special role. So here as we mix and commingle the experiences of different jurisdictions, international criminal jurisprudence has the opportunity to draw on the best of each system. This has great potential, but it also has dangers. If international justice is to prevail, if it is to command universal respect, then we will adopt the highest common factor of safeguards against miscarriages of justice. What must be avoided at all costs is any temptation to take the easiest route, the lowest common denominator, because by definition these cases that come before you are exceptional cases. This is not a pub brawl, a bank robbery, a shoplifting. In such cases, it's relatively easy to be objective, whether as judge or as jury. The words "innocent until proven guilty" are reasonably simple to apply. Such cases, however important in their own context, cannot be said to affect the life of an entire nation or a people. War crimes are different. In the everyday context, we have no problem accepting that, yes, policemen do tell lies; sure, victims do make mistakes in identification; but ultimately in those cases, it is the individual and not the system itself that is on trial. The results of conviction or acquittal are usually only of passing interest to the general public. Here we all recognise that what led Haradin Bala to this courtroom is not the path of a common criminal, so-called. No one can deny the justice of the cause for which Haradin Bala took up his gun. What reasonable person could say that the people of Kosovo had no right to defend themselves against that appalling contemporary euphemism, ethnic cleansing? Theirs was truly a cause of the kind contemplated in the preamble to the Universal Declaration, where man was compelled to have recourse as a last resort to rebellion against tyranny and oppression because their human rights were not protected by the rule of law. Seven years later, Haradin Bala is compelled to sit in a war crimes tribunal. Can he expect to receive the same wholehearted and genuine presumption of innocence that we freely give to the woman accused of attempting to murder an abusive husband? We can't pretend that what we are doing is ordinary. War crimes are exceptional and you may be familiar with the English expression that it is the exception that proves the rule. As a child I thought that that was rather a bizarre expression, until I realised that "proves" means in this sense puts to the proof, tests. Exceptional cases such as these actually put to the proof, they put on trial those values that we profess to hold so dear but which unless we test their truth on our own tongues they risk becoming mere platitudes. Those core values that safeguard respect for justice are innocent until proven guilty and its corollary, beyond a reasonable doubt. We will be asking you to consider the evidence presented on behalf of Haradin Bala in that light. He sits here today an innocent man. That's not just a rhetorical expression, it is a fact of legal due process. So far, nothing has been proved against him; the case remains open. Once you have heard the witnesses whom we will be calling on his behalf, we are that you will agree that there is here clearly in this case a case of reasonable doubt. As I mentioned in opening -- in the beginning, Mr. Bala will himself exercise his right to make a statement. We know that you will listen with care to all he has to say and we trust that it will help you understand more about the man who appears before you. We will then be calling a number of people, most of whom come from the villages in upper Drenica, villagers who either supported the KLA or who joined it; however, unlike the Prosecution we do not believe that all KLA supporters are liars, any more than all Cretans are liars. We offer these witnesses worthy of belief. Indeed, you have already heard from one of them because Elmi Sopi, as you recall, was called jointly by Fatmir Limaj and Haradin Bala, and he has already told you that Mr. Bala came to Lapusnik shortly after the 9th of May and that he left at the end of May. And he, Elmi Sopi, from Lapusnik never saw Haradin Bala there again after that. We will be calling, we anticipate today, Shefki Bala, a neighbour but despite his surname not a relative, and a childhood friend of Haradin Bala. He will tell you more about Mr. Bala's medical history. Although not a doctor, he took him -- he took Mr. Haradin Bala to Pristina hospital in 1993 on the occasion of his second heart attack. We will be calling a doctor in the shape of Dr. Fitim Selimi, who is a thoracic surgeon today and at the time was practicing as a doctor and as a human rights activist. As a doctor, he joined the KLA. He collected medical supplies and he provided help to civilians and soldiers in the region of upper Drenica. He ran a makeshift clinic in Shale in the months of June and July of 1998. And Haradin Bala came to him on many occasions there for treatment for his heart condition. We will then call Skender Bylykbashi, who comes from Bajice, the original hometown of Haradin Bala's wife and her family. And he will tell you how Haradin was compelled to move his own family to safety in Bajice -- perhaps I should say relative safety in Bajice in May of 1998. He will also tell you the knowledge he has concerning what Haradin was doing during the months of June and July and his medical condition, as he observed it to be at that time. Mr. Kadri Dugoli, who is another childhood friend who also recalls visiting Haradin Bala in hospital at the time of his heart attack and also gave shelter for a short period to Haradin's family during the war. Avdullah Puka who didn't know Haradin before the summer of 1998, met him when Kumanova brought him to his house in Javor near Luzhnice. Then Ali Thaqi who is from Lapusnik, has known Haradin all his life and remembers also the second heart attack that Haradin suffered in 1993. He remembers seeing Haradin in Lapusnik shortly after the 9th of May. Finally we intend to call Ferat Sopi, who you recall has been mentioned already as operating the clinic in Lapusnik. He will tell you when he opened that clinic and who he worked with. There will be other evidence that will affect Mr. Bala's case, but those are the live witnesses whom we propose to call. We served notice of alibi well before the beginning of this case, and of course once that is raised in evidence, as it will be by our witnesses, it falls to the Prosecution to disprove beyond a reasonable doubt the validity of that alibi. The burden is not, of course, on the accused. And the sense in which this is an alibi case is in the sense that of evidence that tends to show that by reason of the presence of the defendant in a particular area at a particular time, he was not or was unlikely to have been at the place where the offence is alleged to have been committed at the time that it was committed. This is not a case of a man who was under the care of the state in a hospital, a prison, the army, or any other location where records were kept. So we have no one to bring before you to say on the 25th and 26th of July beyond any question, here is the paper that proves where Haradin Bala was. But there are two compelling factors, we submit, that suggest very strongly why this alibi, so-called, is one on which you can place reliance and one which the Prosecution will be unable to disprove. Those two factors are Mr. Bala's health and his location. Again, we cannot say that it would have been physically impossible for Haradin Bala to perform the actions that he is accused of performing, not impossible, but his health condition makes it highly, highly unlikely that he could or would have been in a position to perform Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those actions. Secondly, his location. After the initial fighting in Lapusnik, the evidence will show that he was given another task by the KLA because of his age and because of his physical infirmity. He was moved to a logistics role in the village of Luzhnice. He needed to make regular visits to the doctor at the clinic in Shale. And we have to bear in mind the overall context of the wartime conditions prevailing. Travel was particularly difficult and dangerous. The doctor who treated him will tell you why he has no medical records that he can call on, again because of the wartime conditions, because of what happened to his clinic when the Serbs finally broke through and committed the atrocities they were able to commit at the end of July. And an additional aspect to the alibi, of course, when a person raises an alibi they say "I wasn't there," "it wasn't me." "Whoever the witness says did it, they've got the wrong person." So the other element relating to that of the alibi is identification, the reliability of those witnesses who have told you it was Haradin Bala who did this to me or to somebody else. And you will hear testimony that those identifications are totally unreliable. An expert upon whom this Tribunal has every reason to rely will say that these identifications are ones on which you cannot safely rely. And in conclusion, may I say a few words about the corollary of the burden of proof and the presumption of innocence, and that corollary of course is proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Mr. President, when you made reference last week to the fact that you and your colleagues are not a raw jury, you underlined an important advantage that Judges have in sorting the wheat from the chaff, the meaningful from the irrelevant. That advantage enables you to recognise, for instance, that documents the Defence would normally seek to exclude in a jury trial may sometimes - I do not say always - may sometimes be safely admitted here. They can be examined and then quietly consigned to the large pile of irrelevant papers marked "not wanted on voyage" when you begin to analyse what is actually of any evidentiary value in this case. But there are times when all of us as advocates and as Judges, too, need to stand back from our professional self-confidence, times when we are in danger of being too comfortably part of the cozy lawyers' world that is alien to that raw jury, times when we must think particularly of the wider public interest that we are called here to serve. It may be that the people of Kosovo need a truth and reconciliation commission among South African lines, but of course this trial cannot be such a commission. The truth that we seek here is what the great legal scholar and judge Albi Sachs of the South African Constitutional Court has called a microscopic truth. As he says: "In a court of law, we apply a kind of technical legalism that is appropriate when you are dealing with the due process of law. You cannot convict without proper testimony, proper cross-examination, without narrow, microscopic examination. And applying this forensic microscope in an objective fashion is a reasonably straightforward exercise when the charge is shoplifting or even murder in the everyday social context. Reasonable doubt is relatively easily understood by judge or jury, but the more serious the crime, the graver the implications for society as a whole. And the graver the implications, the greater our emotional need to see retribution for that crime." The very term "war crimes" is highly emotive. Sitting in The Hague today we are hundreds and hundreds miles distant from the daily reality of Kosovo. Those of us who have been to Kosovo and seen it for ourselves recognise this is another place, another world entirely. And we are seven years distant from the horrors, the chaos, and the anarchy that engulfed the region in 1998. This Tribunal is serviced by a vast engine of investigators, analysts, and prosecutors doing their best to uncover past disappearances and solve past murders. You, as Judges, have a mission to do justice by the international community and by all the people of Kosovo. In order to do this we know that you have made personal and professional sacrifices yourselves. We have come to this Defence bar to perform a service to the cause of international human rights as well. Like you, we wish to see the highest standards of due process safeguarded and not diluted in the face of the most serious criminal charges a person can have to deal with. So please forgive me when I underscore the words "beyond a reasonable doubt." When you have heard all of the evidence in relation to Haradin Bala, we submit there will be at least three areas of evidence that will give you pause: The alibi evidence in its general sense and in the overall context of prevailing wartime conditions in Kosovo, he was not there; the evidence of his health when measured against the considerable physical exertions that had to have accompanied the acts alleged against him, he could not reasonably be expected to have done them; and finally, the so-called identification evidence which will show that no witness made an identification of Haradin Bala upon which any reasonable Tribunal could rely. It was not him. So on behalf of our team, I thank you for your patience and your courtesy for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Now, Mr. Bala, we understand from your counsel that you wish to make a statement. You no doubt have been advised that it is open to you to do that and that if you do make a statement not on affirmation, that you will not be able to be cross-examined by the Prosecution on that statement. Do we understand you wish to make a statement now? THE ACCUSED BALA: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is my wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think because of the need for the microphone to catch you, it would be best if you simply sat in your seat as near to the microphones as you comfortably can and please then make your statement. If the microphone between you and Mr. Limaj could be switched on. Please proceed. You understand you need to speak reasonably slowly because of the interpretation. THE ACCUSED BALA: [Interpretation] I will do my best to do that. Good afternoon, Your Honours. It is the first time in my life that I address a Court. It is the first time in my life that I speak before a microphone, and therefore I would like you from the very beginning to ask your forgiveness for any mistakes because, as you know, I have only completed elementary school. And therefore, I apologise for any possible mistakes from the beginning. It's been six months and some days that we've been sitting in this courtroom, and we almost know each other here by first and last names; but however, I would like again for the record to state my name. As you already know, my name is Haradin Bala. I come from the village of Korretice e Eperme, which is in Drenoc municipality. I am father of ten children, of whom seven are living and three have died. Of my seven living children, I have five daughters and two sons. One of my daughters, who is now 25 years old, was born healthy but unfortunately she fell sick in the age of seven months. And to this date, she is paralyzed, cannot move and cannot control herself. I have, as I said, two sons, the older being 18 years old and the younger 11 years old. I come from a country which has always been poor, a country that has always been occupied by foreigners. Honourable Judges, you have already learned the history of that nation, the suffering of our people, the suppression that it lived in for years. As I said, I come from a very small country, from Kosova, which has a very fertile land and also gold mines, despite being a small country. And foreigners envied her just because of this, because of things she had, and it's because of this that the nation was suffering. For many years before and even today, I think there was a slogan that we used which was: "Trepca Works and Belgrade Builds." If this was the only problem that we had, a problem of poverty, we would have got over it, that wouldn't have been a problem for us. But violence, repression, maltreatment on the streets, in our homes, wherever we were, imprisonments, massive imprisonments, this is what they did to us. A country which had laws, which recognised international human rights and -- not to continue because I don't even know what in all as a country it knew and recognised; however, I would like to say that the suffering of my people in that small country, I heard about this suffering from elderly persons, from my father, from my relatives, old men, who spoke of their suffering. I too suffered what they suffered in the past. I'm not a historian, but you don't need to be educated to know these things that I've mentioned. These are things that everybody knows. Every person who has not completed any school knows these things because these persons suffered these things, they felt them in themselves. As far as I know and as far as I can say with respect to what I heard from my grandfathers, my father, what I've seen myself, if I were to recount to you, Your Honours, everything I know I have heard, I would have needed a lot of time, as long as the Milosevic trial is taking, because there is a lot to say. You don't need a lot of schooling and education to do that, to have finished university, to tell what a country like mine has gone through. I will try, however, to be as brief as I possibly can to concentrate more on my own family. But when I talk about my family, about what it went through, Your Honours, you should rest assured that the majority of the people I come from have gone through the same hardships and suffered the same fate. The differences between -- among our fates are minor. After the end of the Second World War, my grandfather, Haradin Bala - he had the same name as myself - he was forced to leave his home, to leave his property and go to Albania for the sole purpose of escaping Serb brutality. He lived in Albania for 14 years. When he went to Albania, he did the same thing as we did when we took to the mountains, he took with him only his personal belongings; he left behind his whole wealth and property. He left behind 10 acres of land, of fertile land, which even today remain in the hands of Serb occupiers. Even though we had been asking for the restitution of that property, we have not yet received it. That was a wealth which could feed our families for generations. And to this day, we don't have it. Today in Korretice, where I live, I have five brothers and four sisters, and we all share 9 acres of land where our households are built. You may imagine for yourselves what kind of life we can lead in these circumstances, living only on 9 acres of land, nine brothers and sisters together. After 14 years, when my grandfather came back from Albania, he was accused -- my father was accused of -- he was accused in a time which for us was known as the Rankovic time, where we were forced to flee in a large scale. He was accused of staging, of organising, the people to demand the use of the Albanian flag. They accused him of that because they told him, You have lived in Albania and you want to do this now here? That was of course a fabricated charge against him and for that he was sentenced with imprisonment. He was sentenced to two years of imprisonment and three years under house arrest. And I remember very well the time when he was under house arrest because I could see, I was a child, but we could see that he stayed at home night and day, never left home. Your Honours, I told you that you too now know that the military service in the former Yugoslav army was compulsory for Albanian youths. Many Albanians who did that service, that is the military service, in the army of the state, which was known for that army, returned to us as dead persons. They were returned to the families in sealed coffins. The families were not allowed to see whether the -- whether the corpses were inside the coffins. The same fate happened to befall to my younger brother, Abedin Bala. That day when he dressed his civilian clothes and he was greeting his friends to return home where the entire family was waiting for him, on that same day he was arrested. So they arrested him, and he was arrested by a state that had laws. And he was deprived of his fundamental right to live by that state that did not allow him and others like him to be educated in their mother tongue. The forces of that state stopped him in the street whenever they saw him for the only reason that he didn't speak Serbian and that he was Albanian. The police officers of that state beat him and tortured him. I don't think there is any other people in the world that knows how to maltreat and torture others like the Serb people; for us, they are such -- such tortures are well-known. So they arrested him. They poisoned him, they poisoned the people in schools. The same state, the same officers, the same regime imprisoned him. In that notorious jail, they killed him. When we went to fetch his corpse, the only reason they gave us Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for his death, which was not only his death but the death of many other Albanians, was that he has committed a murder. What happened to my brother, Hamdi -- this was told to my brother Hamdi when he went to take his dead body. They told him that Abedin was imprisoned in isolation. In the morning of the 12th January of 1985, 1985, the cook took his breakfast in the cell and saw him lying in the bed covered with a sheet. He thought that he was sleeping. He removed his sheet from his body and when he did so, the cook said that he saw that Abedin had hanged himself with a piece of the sheet. How is it possible for somebody to commit suicide, to hang himself with a piece of sheet and then to fall on the same bed, to cover himself with this sheet? I think this deserves no comment. The grief for our family was great. My father was a folk singer, he used to sing; but after that, he stopped singing. He was unable to sing anymore. Not only then but all the time it was clear to us what was happening. But every family suffered a similar tragedy like my family. I wouldn't say all, but most of our families suffered the same fate. But often we didn't even dare speak with each other or tell each other what had befallen us. We didn't know what to do, how to find a way out of this situation, but at that time we were not as united as we were in 1998 when we got together. Your Honours, when I tell you this maybe someone might think that I'm saying that all the Serbs are responsible for the bad conduct of their government. I have not blamed and do not blame rank-and-file people, ordinary people, irrespective of their religion or the group they belong to, those who tried to cooperate with their neighbours, despite the religion of their leaders. Your Honours, in this very courtroom every day I am sitting in the chair that I am sitting now which is the same chair, the same seat where a monster and not a human being sits, a man who is being tried for trying to exterminate my people from the face of the earth and from human memory through massacres, bloodsheds; through torching their homes, destroying their homes; through forcing hundreds and thousands of people to flee that small country. And he managed to force them -- some of them to flee and the others take to the mountains. Your Honours, maybe to you it may sound strange, but the torture I feel every day when I think that I am sitting in the same place where a barbarian sits, who is being tried for crimes that history of mankind has never heard of. And then when the Prosecution is trying to treat me in the same way as him. I want to tell you one more thing, that when I was telling you about my paralyzed daughter, I want to tell you that it is hard to be such a parent. It is very hard indeed because for 25 years she has never been able to touch the ground with her feet. Today she is lying in bed and every time she is changed her clothes -- along with her clothes we rip parts of her body, of her flesh, and still I can put up with it. When I'm saying this, I don't want to show my disrespect for the Tribunal because I have the greatest of respect personally for this Tribunal, but the entire people expect -- respects it and expects it -- expects much from it. Saying this, I want to tell you, Your Honours, that how can I be sitting in the same place, in the same Trial Chamber with Milosevic, even though we sit at different times, when that person is known on international scale as a barbarian person and when in my case, apart from the charges brought against him, I was looked upon as a liberator by my people? This really hurts me and pains me more than anything. As I said, I live in Korretice e Eperme; it's a valley on which on the 9th of May, Your Honours, I saw flames coming from Lapusnik. I heard the gunshots. The distance is not that great. It seemed as if it was coming from my own courtyard. During that fighting, brave young men had taken part, young men who, as we say back home, has not shaved yet. They were there facing their enemy; they won that battle. I decided to join these young men. When I made my decision, I familiarised one of my brothers with my decision and told him that I will go and join them. He said to me, No, don't go. Give me your weapon and I will go instead of you. You know your situation. You cannot carry 5 kilogrammes of paint and point walls in order to provide for your family; what can you do there? What he was saying was true. However, I had this wish to at least die together with these young men, to at least try and provide safety for my brothers who were at home because as I was more aged than them I believed that they will live to enjoy freedom, and this was the reason I decided to join. It was morning, around 4.00 a.m. when I arrived at Lapusnik. I met those young men that I mentioned, but as we say in our country, they looked as young children. But I looked even older from my actual age because of the suffering and because of my health. Even those young men told me that -- in fact it was Ymer Alushani who said to me that I looked older. I knew Ymer from before. He said to me, Why did you come here? You have many brothers. You should have given this weapon to one of your brothers. And my reply was, No, Ymer. I don't want a freedom without these young men. I don't want to sit and watch these young men get killed. I will do my best to my condition to contribute. And he said to me, But you know yourself. You know that you are not able even to walk or escape. And I said to him, Yes, that's true, but you should know one thing. There were three others there. And I said to him, Wherever I sit, there it's either that I will survive or die. Don't leave me. I joined the KLA, as I said earlier, to provide safety for other brothers because those, those who took up weapons, they all knew that they were in fact killed. We didn't say to ourselves, Okay, let us take up weapons and by God we won't get killed. Everybody knew that death was awaiting them somewhere. From time to time and in different periods of time, they managed to get weapons and to join the KLA as well. In other words, from May until the end of the war, I participated in the war together with four brothers of mine and two nephews, two sons of my brother. I stayed in Lapusnik for around two weeks. Commander Kumanova came. At that time, we didn't know each other as commanders, but now I use the term "commanders" because now we know. At that time, we were soldiers and we respected each other as per the tradition we Albanians have. You pay respect for the elderly persons. We spoke with him. We informed him. He understood my health condition. He asked me to accompany him to together with him because as he said, You are in a very dangerous place and perhaps you will be more of assistance to us in another place than here now that you have made up your mind to help our army, our liberation army. And that's why I went with him there to Luzhnice. In this courtroom, I've heard many testimonies of people who accused me of beating them, of opening and closing doors so others could beat them, of executing my own people; this is not true. Your Honours, I did not do these things. The things that happened to these people worry me a lot, they make me very sad. I do not know why they think I was involved. But, Your Honours, you will probably remember that another person was brought here before this Court; he was arrested by the OTP and brought to the Tribunal. Many of those who came here to testify, they claim that I was present there as well and that I was involved in things that I am accused of doing. A mistake has been made here, Your Honours. I was not involved in these things. I don't know that such things happened, Your Honours, and I don't believe that a single person from our own people would do things as we are accused of. I have a deep respect for NATO and the forces that saved my country and helped the KLA to protect its people from a total extermination by Milosevic. Your Honours, please understand that the day will come when all Kosovars living in Kosova, boys and girls, men and women, they will stand together as one, as an independent nation with all its constituent groups living a free life, working together for the betterment of all the people, not only part of them. Your Honours, in the end I would like to say that I respect you greatly and that I'm grateful for being given the opportunity to address you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That is clearly a convenient time for the first break. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could call Mr. Shefki Bala, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take this opportunity to greet Your Honours, all the parties here, and my co-patriots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bala.

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Where do you presently live?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I live in Korretice e Eperme, Drenoc municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to stand closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could, there's been a request that you sit a little closer to the microphone because I think you might have a low voice. And how long have you lived there, sir?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I was born there and I live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I have known him since our childhood. We've been together in the high school -- sorry, during the high school age. All the time we've been together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I notice that your last name is Bala, as is his. Are you related to each other?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: We live in the same neighbourhood. We are neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if you could tell us, how big a village do you live it? How big is Korretice?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Korretice is large. It has about 4 or 500 houses. I can't tell you how large it is in terms of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, since you've known Haradin Bala all your life, could you tell me, are you taller than he is, shorter than he is, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I am taller than Haradin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you by any chance know about how tall you are?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I am 1 metre, 75 or 80 centimetres tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by any chance, do you know what colour his eyes are?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Usually these are things which we don't look at, but I think they are light blue or green.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. During the time that you've known Haradin Bala, do you know whether or not he ever worked?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Yes. He has worked in the 1980s in a construction company in Drenoc, former Gllogovc. He was a painter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you know, how long he worked as a painter?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: He worked there for as long as that enterprise existed, and then it went bankrupt and all the workers were fired; he suffered the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After the business he worked for went bankrupt, do you know what he did next for a job?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I think he was a good worker, a capable person in that profession and he was much sought after. He didn't have a regular job, but he had plenty of work, one day, two days, maybe a week, but he didn't have a regular job.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, directing your attention to the 1990s, was he working during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: In the 1990s, Haradin did the same job but he didn't have a lot Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of work because -- he couldn't work much because he was ill, that's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You say that he couldn't work much because he was ill. Is there a specific date or time when you recall him becoming ill?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I think it was in 1993. I don't remember the exact date. It must have been the end of July and the beginning -- the end of June and the beginning of July. I took him in my own car to a clinic, first aid clinic, in Prishtine because there was a police checkpoint at Komorane, a Serb police checkpoint, and we were forced to go to Prishtine. We were afraid to go to Drenoc where there was another clinic because of that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you took him in our own car to Prishtine, why did you take him in your car to a clinic? Was there something that had happened? Was there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: The reason for that was that the health state institutions didn't pay much attention to such grievances at that time. So we -- the citizens or the villagers had to take care of themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was there something -- some reason that he needed to be taken care of? Was something going on with him at that point in time that required you to take him in a car to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I felt it my obligation -- in fact, not only for Haradin but for all my co-villagers. This was something that we used to do at that time quite often because if I myself were in the same situation, I was sure that Haradin would do the same for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What situation was Haradin in at that time that you took him to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I was returning from work where I was working in agriculture. It was about 4.00 and I heard a voice coming from Haradin's yard. I went to see what was happening. He was having a great pain in his chest and I told him, Let's go to the doctor. But he didn't want to go to the doctor. So we insisted on his going to the doctor, to the clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it you were successful in getting him to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I said that we convinced him to go and see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you learn whether or not the -- him complaining about a pain in his chest meant anything?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: In the clinic in Lipjan, in Prishtine, they gave him the first aid. But the doctor said he should be taken to the hospital, to the ward that deals with internal diseases. I don't know much of medicine but then the doctor later on told us that he had sort of infarction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You said that he had a sort of infarction. Is that a heart attack that you're referring to or some other kind of heart condition?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: The nurse told us this and then it was proven afterwards that he was suffering from infarction because immediately they put him to some equipment there. I don't know what they are, some heart equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you remember how long he stayed in the hospital that time?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I told you earlier that I cannot remember some details, but I think he must have stayed about 15 days more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After he came back from the hospital, do you recall whether he continued to work as a painter or not?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: No, but I do remember that he didn't work but that he asked for assistance in the Albanian state, that is he went there for further treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that he didn't work but he asked for further assistance, do you personally have any knowledge about he -- how he was able to support his family at that time?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I may tell you that he had a very difficult life. It was with difficulty that he survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On a side note, did you know his father?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Yes, pretty well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What did his father do?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: His father received a small pension, but they are many brothers and Haradin had his own house, but his father used to sing folk songs. He was a singer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to 1998, and specifically sometime around the month of May. Did you have occasion to see Haradin at that time in the village of Korretice?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: I frequently met him until May every day I would say, until May of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there come a time in May when you no longer saw him in Korretice?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: After the Likoshan event, our village, too, was engaged in self-organisation. We started to keep guard of the village at night until May. And even though Haradin was ill he too wanted to join in that organisation. And we watched -- we stayed on guard together. We just kept vigil. We didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did Haradin remain in the village of Korretice throughout the month of May?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: After the Lapusnik battle, that is after the 9th of May, Haradin's brothers told me that he had joined the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After Haradin Bala left, after the battle of Lapusnik on the 9th of May, when did you see him again?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: In -- on the 10th of August of 1998 I went to Germany with my family. And after the 9th of May, I remember I have seen him after I returned from Germany in November of 1999. I didn't see them at other times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may wait there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Nor I. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you've known Haradin Bala since childhood as a neighbour?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as a friend of your family's?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell me the names of his four brothers who also took part in the war?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. Apart from Haradin, it was Fatmir, Fadil, Bahtir, and the youngest, Besim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know, if you can tell me, approximately when these four men were born or how old they are now, whichever is easier for you.

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: No problem. I can tell you approximately what their ages. I don't know their birth dates, however I'll do my best. Bahtir is 69 born; Fadil, 77; Fatmir, 72; and Besim, at the most born in 1979, around these years [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I believe that Haradin Bala had two nephews who also fought or took part in the war. Can you tell me their names and about when they were born.

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Which nephews are you referring to? Because he has many nephews. I know their names, but his nephews might be Kadri and Ali who joined the ranks. But as I said, Haradin has many nephews.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the two, if you know, who joined the ranks of the KLA. And if it was Kadri and Ali, could you tell me when they were born?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Uh-huh, just a moment. I need to clarify things here because we call nephews the children of our sisters or of the sisters of our parents. And here you refer to his brother's son. In this case, it's Agron and Jeton.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when were they born, please?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Agron could have been born in 1970, 1972, same generation as Fatmir; while Jeton around 1972 -- 1977, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who is their father, Agron and Jeton?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Haradin's oldest brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what's his name?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Hamdi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've talked a little bit about how you helped Haradin Bala. You took him to the doctor in 1993 and you've also loaned him money for medical treatment at one stage, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said you took Haradin Bala to the doctor in your car. Did Haradin Bala have a car in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Haradin didn't have a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did he have a Lada in 1998 or use of a Lada in 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: His younger brothers used some cars, but Haradin did not have a personal car. I'm not sure whether he had one, but as I said his brothers used cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked about Haradin Bala painting houses, working in the building trade, and then being dismissed. That happened to lots of people at this time, didn't they? Many Albanian men were dismissed from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Haradin remained without a job, and it is true that he didn't have a job afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And my point is that that was true of many men, whether they were ill or not, had to work part-time jobs to survive?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: The occupying system in Kosova was a social system. And to tell you the truth, just a small number of Albanians could get employed within this system. Even those who were employed in 1974 with the fall of the constitution, the amendments, many Albanians lost their jobs and those who got jobs actually, as I said, were small in number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And after 1993, Haradin Bala did what he could to help his family, didn't he, although he wasn't working regularly?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: That is correct. And there's another truth, too. We citizens helped them, relatives, nephews, uncles. Haradin was not in a situation to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Haradin Bala was one of the people in Korretice who organised a village defence guard in March of 1998. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: Haradin was, but he was not part of the organising the defence. Other villagers were part of the organisation. I can mention Sherif Hoxha, Zymer Shabani, Mehmet Xharahi and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. But he was part of that original village defence guard?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: As I said earlier, and I will repeat it, we were just observing in the village. Our village comprises several neighbourhoods. We stood guard duty in Bala neighbourhood. With him, I was in the same shift. We would observe for two hours together, just in case anything happened, so that we would be awake and not asleep as events in Prekaz and Likoshan happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Haradin's older brother, Hamdi, did he join the KLA in 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: No, he didn't join. He lives in Switzerland and he was in Switzerland for that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For the entire war?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: For the entire war he was in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Haradin Bala in May, as we've heard, took up his rifle to go to Lapusnik when there was fighting there. I just want to be clear. Is that something you just heard about or did you see him leaving to go to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SHEFKI BALA
utterances.text: As I said earlier, and I will repeat it, during the first battle at Lapusnik, Haradin informed me and said to me he was going to see what were the news there after the battle ended. I later on did not see Haradin but I was informed by his brothers that he joined the KLA ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bala.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bala. You're now able to leave the court and return to your home. The officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I greet you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next witness will be Dr. Fitim Selimi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, the next witness will be Fitim Selimi, and Mr. Harvey will be examining him. We're trying to give you a bit of variety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Selimi.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot here the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Can you state --

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Fitim Selimi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: If you could move a little bit closer. The interpreters are having a little bit of difficulty hearing you speaking. Okay. Thanks very much. And you're a doctor of medicine?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you have a particular medical specialty?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: A thorax surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just waiting for it to come up on the screen in front of me. And where did you study to obtain your medical qualifications?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I studied at the Pristina University Faculty of Medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And in which year did you qualify?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I completed my studies in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When did you first begin at the university?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I began in 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Between 1980 and 1993, were your studies interrupted?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, they were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And what caused that interruption?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: My studies were interrupted due to the fact that there was a situation which was for all other Albanians as well, and I was imprisoned as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: For what offence were you sent to prison?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I was imprisoned on the basis of charges fabricated by the Serbian regime, which was collaboration in ruining the sovereignty of the Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. We have an approximate translation here, but I think we can work with that. Do you know what articles of the constitution you're alleged to have violated or what articles of the Penal Code?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: We were working only for the freedom of our people. We didn't violate any articles. We were accused under Article 136 of the Yugoslav constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And were you accused of any acts of violence at all?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No. We articulated our just demands as a people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when did you get out of prison?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I got out of prison after two years, that is in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Were you required to do military service?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: You mean in the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: They forced me to do my military service in Karlovce by the end of September, 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Is that in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, in Croatia -- 1988, correction, was the year of the military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So you came out of prison in 1988. You went into the JNA. While you were in the JNA, did you -- were you required to use your medical skills in any way?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: In conformity with my profession, I was profoundly discriminated there. But after four months, reason prevailed, probably, and I was engaged to work in the military clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When you came -- when did you come out of the military, which month, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: After one year. It was September 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And did you return to the University of Pristina at that point?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I returned to my hometown.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was there a particular reason why you didn't go back to the University of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I wanted to go back to studies and I used to read a lot at home, but at that time the university was closed down and all the cadres were dismissed from work and so we had to take a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So you had to pursue your studies from home?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: During that period, were you politically active again?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was active.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In which organisation or organisations?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: In the beginning of the 1990s, I was involved in the political organisation of the LDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When did you pick up your studies again?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I picked up my studies again by the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you've told us that you graduated in 1993. That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: At that point, of course, you were qualified. Now, were you permitted by the Serbian authorities to practice medicine in a public hospital or any hospital or clinic under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. I was qualified. I was graduated in a school where professors, well-known professors, taught. Now the situation changed. Those professors, those cadres were working outside the institution. They were conducting an independent activity in terms of education.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And what did that mean in terms of your employability?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: In terms of our employability, it meant that our diplomas were not valid in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So where did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: We practiced our professions wherever we could, in our hometowns, in various humanitarian institutions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And your hometown was where?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: My hometown is Banulle, a village in the vicinity of Lipjan, a small town, not far from Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And did you operate a clinic or any form of medical practice from your home in Banulle?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. At various points of time I was active. I may say that I was operating all the time from my home, caring for people who needed medical help.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you could operate -- work with various humanitarian institutions. Did you work -- did you work for any humanitarian organisation?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I worked for a time for Mother Teresa; it was a charity organisation. And then for a time I was the director of the International Red Cross branch in Lipjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: For how long did you work for the Mother Teresa organisation?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: For two or three years in a row.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So does that start in 1993 or when?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1993 until 1997 with -- on and off I have worked in these institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when you were directing the Red Cross, was that the same period of time?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you work with or give assistance to any international human rights organisations during this period?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: The situation where -- we were in was such that the only way to give vent to our aspirations was through international institutions like the Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, and others like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Were there any local what you might call home-grown human rights organisations in Kosovo at that time?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, there were local organisations which tried to voice the injustices committed against the Albanian population in Kosova during that time, such as the Council for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms, which I founded first and then directed for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Approximately when were you involved in the founding and direction of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: The founding of that council was done in 1993, at the -- by the end of 1993 with the initiate of Ademi Demaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, so far we've been talking largely the period from 1993 to 1997. Did a change come about in -- towards the end of 1997/beginning of 1998?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. The situation in Kosova was deteriorating. For most of the population, that was an unacceptable situation. People started to think differently. The political entities that were formed and leading the life of the people were losing their authority because of the passive policy they were pursuing which led to the violation of the rights of the Albanians. This led to many people fleeing Kosova. This was about -- the number was about 30 per cent of the most active and vital part of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, the Tribunal of course has heard a lot about the massacres that occurred in March in 1998 in Drenica. Did those massacres have any impact on your work and what you did with your life from that point onwards?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Certainly they did. We had to be or were those who had to take the lead and articulate the demands of the people, trying to help, to relieve the situation which was very grave for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When you say "we," who do you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I mean the Albanian people of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When you say "we had to take the lead," who took the lead?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I mean especially those people who had education, who were trained for such days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: This period -- let's talk of the period March through May of 1998, for example. What was the functioning of normal society in the area in which you were living and working? In other words, to make the question a bit clearer, perhaps: Were schools functioning normally? Were people -- were people -- the elderly receiving pensions and state payments? Were medical facilities functioning normally, or was it different?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Normality was beyond the question, not only during that period but beginning from 1989 onwards. The educational institutions were not functioning. The factories and the plants were not functioning. Neither was health service. That the situation reached the worst point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: How did people get food, clothing, medical supplies during this period? Again, I'm talking now of March to May of 1998.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: During that period the situation was very grave, especially for people living in the zones involved in the conflicts. The only way to survive for them was to get supplies from other parts of Kosova, thanks to the self-organisation of the people in these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When -- when you mentioned that you were in Lipjan, is that one of the areas that you are talking about as a zone involved in conflict?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: The territory of Lipjan was an area where following the incessant attacks in Drenica, a large number of people had left as refugees, in Kroimire, Shale, Bajice, Fushtice villages. There were 1.400 people who had come from other areas as a result of being suppressed and persecuted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So you had an influx of refugees from Drenica?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. There was a flux -- a large flux of refugees. Therefore, we had to merge all the political efforts to set up a non-political body that would operate to resolve the numerous problems facing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And were you involved in setting up that body?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was. I was leading the health sector within the emergency council; that was the structure -- a structure to deal with emergency situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, I can't help noticing that you've taken out a document of some sort. Is that a document to which you need to refer for the purposes of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I have a document here which mentions the number of people who were dismissed, who were maltreated in the police, and other such things. If you think I might -- it's relevant for me to use it, I might submit it. During this time, over 700.000 Albanians were maltreated by the police. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that. For the time being, I'm not -- since I don't know what the document is, I don't particularly ask to see it. It may be that the Prosecution may wish to look at it. But if you just put the documents on one side for a moment, I -- let me just ask you this: You said that that document, whatever it is, refers to numbers of people who have been maltreated by the police.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Were you involved in collect -- in treating people who had been maltreated by the police or in collecting evidence from them at any stage?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I was. During that time, we wanted to help all those people who were maltreated in various ways. The Council for Human Rights and Freedoms in Lipjan submitted to various bodies, international bodies and organisation, a file with names and photos of the people who were mistreated and maltreated. I was involved personally in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I see. Well, I'm not seeking to put that before the Tribunal at this stage, but that is work -- that's part of the work you were doing with your humanitarian organisational work?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And during what period of time were you collecting that evidence of people's abuses?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: They -- the evidence dates from 1981 onwards, including the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I think you were telling us about the work that -- an organisation that was created to deal with the refugees who came flooding into the Lipjan municipality. Did that organisation have a name?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't exclusively created to treat refugee problems. It was an organisation that was established due to the existing circumstances which would be as an organisation in a situation to provide assistance for refugees, soldiers, and all those who would be in motion for the freedom. This was an emergency council which became functionable by offering assistance not only to the civilian population but also to the KLA army which had begun to have a more active role.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When was this emergency council set up, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: It was set up in mid-March 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was it set up by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No, it was set up by the people. It included representatives of different political bodies who, in a way, merged together. There were members from the LDK, representatives of a finance council of the municipality, of education council of the municipality, members of parliamentary parties, and all other political and non-political bodies that were active in Kosova at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And what did you personally do on behalf of the emergency council?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Having in mind the escalation of the situation, I specifically dealt with collecting the material, equipment, and medicaments. Within the framework of this emergency council, I worked in the health department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So when you speak of material and equipment, are you speaking of health material and equipment or any other kind of health -- any other kinds of equipment?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I mainly or exclusively speak of equipment and supplies, medical equipment and supplies, that would be necessary for the treatment of the population and the army at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you yourself were invited to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't wait to join the KLA ranks, and this resulted in an invitation that was given to me by my cousin, Shukri Buja, the son of my uncle. He wanted to meet me. And on this meeting, he offered me the possibility to get involved directly and help and provide assistance for the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did Shukri Buja tell you what kinds of help and assistance the KLA needed from you?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: This perhaps needs a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that the institutions had functioned in a way until that time and as of then they had lost connections with their base, the civilian population living in the zones where the KLA had emerged did not have any help or assistance, including medical help. Therefore, Shukri's initiative was for me to go there and, in a way, work and engage myself in providing medical care for that population there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And where was -- where are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: We're talking about the zone covering some villages starting from the village of Pjetershtice, Kroimire, Shale, Bajice, Klecke, and other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And -- so what did you do, having joined the KLA at Shukri's request and agreed to provide assistance? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: From that moment, I took care of everything that we had at our disposal, material, supplies, equipments, to place those in zones where there was a number, a significant number of KLA members, and put them in the service of the population and the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Were there medical facilities already established that you were able to use or did you have to set them up afresh?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: The existing institutions that -- until that time were administered by the Serbian regime, as was the Shale outpatient clinic, they were abandoned. And someone had to take over the administration of these institutions. We were based in Shale, at Shale outpatient clinic. From there we provided medical assistance to those who needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What you refer to as an outpatient clinic, or what at least has been translated as an outpatient clinic, you use the word "ambulans," I believe, in Albanian. Are we talking about something that is sophisticated or what?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No. We are talking of improvisation that were imposed on us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: From the -- oh, I don't think you've given us the date on which you joined the KLA.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: The date was 5th of May, 1998, and from this time onwards until mid-June, maybe 10th or 15th of June, I was mainly working in semi-illegality. During this period I moved from Shale to Lipjan and my house. And in mid-June and onwards, I settled within the KLA ranks, where I remained until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So during -- dealing with the period 5th of May through 10th or 15th of June, as you were moving around, what were you doing? Were you moving people? Were you moving medical supplies? What -- where were you going, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: During this time, we mainly collected and transported sanitary equipment from another zone. In a way, it was a freedom of movement. So from one zone to the zone of Drenica e Eperme, concretely in Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Drenica e Eperme, that means upper Drenica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I referred to those few Drenica villages that belonged to Lipjan municipality, Kroimire, Shale, and Pjetershtice, which actually belongs to Shtime municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was Lapusnik one of the villages that you were responsible for assisting in any way?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: We did not have the possibility to do that. I was mainly involved in Shale of Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In Shale, you said you had your clinic there. Was -- well, just dealing with this whole area of upper Drenica, was any -- was the KLA in total control of that area? Were the Serbs in control of that area? Was anyone in control of that area at that time? We're talking now really May through July of 1998.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: If it is clear to me what you mean by "controlled by," I can say that the zone was controlled by the population that was there. The KLA consisted of a small number of soldiers. On the other hand, the Serb forces were controlling it from a distance, shelling it every day from their positions such as Goles and other positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So again, during this period of May through July, how safe was it to travel around by car during that period in this region of upper Drenica?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: It wasn't safe to travel by car. The movements of citizens mainly occurred at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When you became more or less full time in Shale, if you had to travel to some other location, let's say Nekovce, how would you travel?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Nekovce is not very far from Shale. Many had the opportunity even to go there on foot but also by other vehicles such as tractors and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What sort of road, path, track was there that you yourself would use during that period?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: The road from Shale to Nekovce is not an asphalt road, a muddy one and full of other obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What about the the road from Shale to Luzhnice?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I didn't go to Luznica at that time but it was also a very difficult path, resembling other paths in that region. When we talk about roads, at that time citizens were mobilised to construct those roads because the movement in main roads was restricted. People had to use mountain roads in order to be able to fulfil their needs for food and clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm going to come now to Haradin Bala. Have you ever met Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
