utterances.text: Which period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: At any time in your life have you ever met Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I first met Haradin Bala during the time that I stayed in Shale. In other words, the period from mid-June to the end of July. I met him several times during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What happened at the end of July?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: At the end of July, the situation was very difficult. The Serb forces had undertaken an offensive against a large number of villages and buildings in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And so what happened to your clinic in Shale at the end of July?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: The clinic in Shale, due to the penetration of Serbian forces in that area, was burned, as were other houses in Shale village. So we were forced to leave the clinic and continue with our activity in the mountains, that is to provide medical help wherever it was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately the date on which you left the clinic in Shale?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: The date when I left the clinic in Shale is easy to remember because of the developments. On this very date, several positions manned by KLA soldiers fell as well. It was the 25th or 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And let's just deal with the week leading up to that, the week leading up to and ending with the 25th and 26th of July. Where -- do you recall now where you were during that week?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: During that week, I was in Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you leave Shale for any reason, as far as you recall, that week?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think so because we had a very large number of patients who needed medical care. The number of doctors was very small; it was only me and two other colleagues. Some of them were engaged in Kroimire, in Pjetershtice. Therefore, during this period I was pretty much linked to Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When you left the clinic, did you leave normally or did you leave in a hurry?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: It was recommended by soldiers, colleagues from the KLA, that the population left the buildings because several KLA positions had fallen and there was a possibility for the worst to happen. So the message was for us to leave the buildings and to flee to the mountains where a number of soldiers would later position as well in order to defend the population in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when you say "necessary for us to leave," is that every living person in Shale or just you in the clinic or what?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: This goes for the entire population, because at that time these buildings were being targeted from distance. The Serb forces were shelling these buildings and therefore the population was forced to take up to the mountains in order to shelter themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I don't know if you can describe for us what that was like at the time, but did people just get up, pack their suitcases, and walk in an orderly fashion, or what did they do?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: During that period, I may tell you that we were the last to leave because we had many injured to take care of because of the shelling. The number of injured people was great. They were put on the trailers. It Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. happened that the shells fell on the trailers of the tractors, and many were wounded, including children and women. So there was total chaos and panic. The citizens were running with children, women trying to get with them from their homes various items like flour or other food supplies which they needed for their life -- for living in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, were you able to take all of your medical supplies with you?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Not -- yes, but not all of them. Since you are asking me, I remember very well that I left behind a microscope and it was destroyed precisely in the place where we were taking care of the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Were you able to take with you any medical records that you had been keeping of your treatment of patients in that clinic while you were in Shale?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No. Maybe some notes we could take with us, but the main records, medical records - and we did have plenty of them - we didn't manage to get them with us. I left behind a number of books. There was a book on surgery, infectious surgery and other books. I left them all behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned that you treated -- or you saw Haradin Bala in Shale between the middle of June and the end of July. Approximately how many times do you recall seeing him during that period?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: The number of visits that Mr. Bala had in our clinic was large because he had frequent complaints with his health. Maybe he came about ten times during that period or even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And was that spread out throughout the period of mid-June to the end of July or was it a concentrated number of visits during a shorter part of that period, if you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I have the impression that the number of visits was spread out from the mid-June until the time when the panic broke out, as I told you earlier. I don't remember the exact dates when he came for a visit, but I know that he came often during all that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So if we're talking of from mid-June through until the 25th or 26th of June, we're talking of a period of something like six or seven weeks. That's not really a leading question; it's just a simple fact. So you're saying about ten times over that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I don't think it's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Sorry, did I answer my own leading question? I probably did. In that case, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You told the Tribunal that you remember Haradin Bala. After treating him those up to ten times, when did you next see him and in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Hadn't I seen Haradin Bala on television when this process started, I don't know when I would see him. That was the first time after that period when I saw him on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What was your reaction when you saw him on television?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I didn't have any particular reaction. I just recalled the patient [realtime transcript read in error: "passion"] who for me was a special one, because it was very rarely or not at all for me at that time to see KLA soldiers come and ask for my assistance on reasons of their health.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You say "on reasons of their health," other than injury caused by being in the war, you mean reasons of bad health. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. Usually the soldiers of the KLA in most cases when they came to ask for assistance, they wanted to be treated for wounds, injuries they inflicted on them during military exercises, that is during combats with the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to pass to the specific complaints for which the Dr. Selimi treated Mr. Bala, so this might be a convenient moment to break if it's convenient to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. We will resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correction to the transcript I think. Line 19 it says he recalled the passion -- person or patient I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We note the passion, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I made the correction automatically, but I'm glad to be corrected. Doctor, we have to have a break now for the tapes to change. We will resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Doctor, when Haradin Bala came to your clinic in June and July of 1998, what medical complaints was he suffering?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Haradin, as I said, had a peculiar health problem. He complained of pain in his chest. He felt weak and tired. It was a general weak condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Had you conducted an examination of him on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. The medical visit consisted of hearing with a stethoscope his heartbeats. We didn't have better equipment to diagnose his health condition, other than hearing his pulse and his beats. At the same time I used to take notes for his medical history, take notes of his problems, whether they were recent or earlier ones. At the same time, I found out that he was taking medicaments for that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you recall as you sit here today whether when he gave you his medical history he told you of any long-standing problems?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that he had long-standing problems and that when he felt these attacks, he used some medicaments which he showed me. He had the medicine with him which he used now and again when he had the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What was that medicine?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: He had nitroglycerine tablets that he used when he had pain in his chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What are nitroglycerine tablets generally used for in the medical profession?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: As a doctor, apart from the clinical symptoms and Mr. Bala's complaints, the explanations he gave me about his medical history, seeing nitroglycerine tablets I realised that he felt pains of the -- related to angina pectoris, which consist of the narrowing of the veins which do not allow the heart muscle to function properly and this results [as interpreted] to other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What effect does nitroglycerine have on constricted veins?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Usually the symptoms that I noted in this patient, in this case Mr. Bala, show that his blood vessels had constricted. And usually the symptoms last up to ten minutes after which the patient either feels better or -- after ten minutes or if he uses nitroglycerine he will feel better earlier because the nitroglycerine extends the blood vessels that are constricted. Usually the blood vessels are constricted up to 50 to 80 per cent of their capacity and the nitroglycerine expands them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And in conducting a physical examination of him, were there any other physical conditions that you noticed about him?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: He was always weak, I mean in terms of his general condition. He could hardly move, could hardly breathe. He has a sort of dyspnoea or a difficult breathing that usually results from that condition. All these symptoms led to insufficiency of the heart muscles. The angina leads to insufficiency. I wasn't in a position at that time with the few appliances and equipment at that time to determine the level of his insufficiency.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: During that period of June to July of 1998, did you treat any other KLA soldiers for heart conditions?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No, no. As I said earlier, usually the soldiers came to me for injuries and wounds, but not for heart diseases. I didn't have any other patient suffering from heart disease.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Again, that word is "patient." Thank you. The fact that he was a serving soldier at that time, did you make any recommendations regarding the duties that it was appropriate for him to perform?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: In such cases, when soldiers were incapable of performing their daily activities, we used to give recommendations. I'm not sure whether I gave him oral or written recommendations in this case. I remember that I recommended that Mr. Bala be involved in slight physical exercises which would save him overexertion because I had, in view of his health condition, I thought that maybe he should leave the army altogether because of that condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you recall in June and July how warm the weather was at that time of year in 1998?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Usually July in our area is a very hot period. It is the peak of hot weather. The temperature, I cannot give you the exact temperature in grades, but usually it reaches up to 30, 35 Celsius.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And do you remember whether that was the case, in fact, in that summer as opposed to in general?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the terrain of the Berisa Mountains?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You of course -- I think you told us you sought refuge there with the many hundreds, if not thousands, of other refugees from the area that you were in?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: How would you describe that terrain from the point of view of which ease a person could walk over that ground?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: In general, the terrain is a rugged terrain with hills, with some sharp peaks, with paths -- narrow paths and tracks which are very hard to go through. It was very difficult for me until I could find my way about that area because it is very difficult terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You found it difficult for yourself?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: How would you describe your state of health in the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I was in very good condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: For somebody in Mr. Bala's condition, bearing in mind his health, that terrain, and that heat, what is your view of the likely impact on him, medically speaking, of having to take, let us say, a walk of some 2, 3, 4 kilometres through the mountains?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Such a health condition as that of Mr. Bala implies that in such circumstances the patient had to avoid extreme temperature, overexertion, especially of the type that was required there. The condition, the terrain would make his condition worse. This is why I recommended to him to go for treatment to some specialised institution and maybe even to leave, as I said, to be released from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you remain there please, Doctor, there will be some more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon Doctor, or good evening. Could you tell me first of all how often you met with Mr. Bala's Defence team in this case - this is just some preliminary questions - prior to your testifying today.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: With Mr. Bala's Defence team I met twice prior to my testifying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was that in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you also meet with them when you arrived here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And there's absolutely nothing wrong with that but you discussed -- they told you about the way things would go in court, where you would sit, and about the way -- the questions that would be asked and what you would testify to?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No. I once said before the lawyers, I repeated my statement that I gave them earlier. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So you gave a statement in Kosovo and then you went over that statement here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To make sure that your answers about Mr. Bala and what you've testified to here today were complete?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as accurate as you could be according to your memory?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you joined the KLA 5th of May, 1998, in Lipjan, and that was through Shukri Buja, your relative? You need to answer verbally. You're shaking your head.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you in contact at that time with Ram Buja as well?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No. At that time I wasn't in contact with Ram Buja.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you -- and that's Shukri Buja's brother?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who is also a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. They are brothers and, as I said, they are the sons of my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you in contact with Ram Buja in June and July of 1998? Did you talk to him at all?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I think I didn't contact Ram Buja. I did contact Shukri. As for Ram, I contacted him later on, after September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where did you -- how did you contact Shukri Buja in June and July 1998? Where did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I met Shukri in May. The first meeting occurred in May and after that I met him every now and then in Shale. He had other duties as well and therefore I could only see him from time to time at the outpatient clinic in Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you joined the KLA, it was on an invitation, I think is the way it was put, from Shukri Buja. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you invite anybody to join the KLA or propose to anybody that they also ought to join as a solution to Kosovo's problems?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: During this time, of course I asked for assistance from other people to help me in collecting supplies and to bring me everything that had to do with logistics, to help me carry out my duties in my sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand as part of that, to carry those duties and accomplish those tasks, you would ask others to join you and to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Either to join the KLA or help the KLA, based on their willingness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked about your background and how there was difficulty in medical school for you studying because of the persecution from the Serb regime. I think you need to speak up just a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And while you were studying at that time when you finished I think you said in 1993, something like that, you were studying for general medicine. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you learned your specialty that you now work in after the war? You trained for this -- your specialty in thoracic surgery?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I specialised -- I began with my specialisation after the war and I completed it two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the time in Shale in your clinic, you've described that as an improvised clinic or hospital.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing like where you work now in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At that clinic, did you have any computerised tools and equipment to help you with diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No, except for manual equipment like stethoscope and the equipment for measuring the blood pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. That's what I mean is you couldn't perform electrocardiograms, things like that?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you couldn't -- I may mispronounce these even in English. You couldn't perform coronary angiography or arteriography, where the -- you understand me. That was impossible?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Right. It wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you couldn't do any computerised exercise stress test to measure the functioning of the heart?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly then, when Mr. Bala -- when Mr. Bala visited you, what name did you know him by, by his pseudonym or by his -- by Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Well, when he introduced himself, I think in our notes we recorded persons with their names and last names. I'm sure that he introduced himself with his full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And my understanding then is when he came in you would listen to his heart with a stethoscope and perhaps take his blood pressure. Right?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he had nitroglycerine pills and you used the medication he had to work back to what the problem must be?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. He informed me that in such situations he took the nitroglycerine pill.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And he wasn't able to provide you with a stack of medical records and x-rays, was he, for you to review?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: This situation occurred many times. During all these visits, I created a full impression about Mr. Bala and I recommended him that he should do all the examinations in proper institutions regarding this health issue. Everything that I determined as a doctor was based on what he told me and based on his history, medical history.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, my question is: Did you have a full written medical history to refer to when you first met him or did you just rely on what he told you his medical history was?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I mainly relied on what he told me and on what my possibilities were at that time in order to make that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said you referred to him, if possible, to go to better-equipped places, hospitals, where they would be able to provide him with better tests and perhaps other medication because you couldn't do that?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It sounds to me from your testimony like every visit from Mr. Bala was pretty close to identical. You would see him, he would complain about some pain, you would observe him, and then send him on his way; you couldn't really help him, could you?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: He was convinced to remain in the KLA ranks. At times, I offered him pills that he lacked. On some occasions, he came to collect nitroglycerine pills which he later used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And despite any of your recommendations, he was determined to remain in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I did not find out about his determination from his statement, but I saw it in the fact that he did not seek for help anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you followed this trial since it began in the press back home or on television or the Internet?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, from time to time but not on regular basis, only when I can follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell us where a Gajrak hospital was near Malisevo somewhere. Are you aware of a hospital with that name or another clinic?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. It existed during the war in municipality of Malisheve, however I didn't go there. I know that a colleague of mine, a doctor, a urologist Agim Hazrolli was his name. He worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you aware in 1998 when Haradin Bala came to visit you that he was a smoker?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he was a smoker or not, but I recommended that he should not smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because for somebody with a heart condition who is a smoker, the single most effective thing they can do on their own is to stop smoking to improve their health. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: It's one of the measures that should be undertaken. I don't remember discussing the smoking issue. But however, we discussed all the measures that he had to undertake in order to improve his condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. But if you had a patient now, not Haradin Bala, visit you, somebody with a serious heart condition and they smoked two packs a day and told you that they had no intention of quitting, you would think that that person wasn't very concerned about their health, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I have many patients to whom I recommend not to smoke. My father died two months ago. He was in a very difficult health and insisted on smoking a cigarette. I didn't try to convince him not to do that. I allowed him to smoke because he was living his last hours. It's very difficult to convince patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That doesn't completely answer my question. If you have a patient who's a heavy smoker with a heart problem, if that person refuses to even try to stop smoking, you would consider them non-compliant with your medical recommendations. Right?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No, that's not what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Somebody who has no intention of stopping smoking when they've been told by their doctor that they ought to and they've got a heart problem, that person is -- you don't consider that somebody who is not complying with their doctor's recommendations?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I see this person as a person who is not complying with doctor's recommendations, but not as a person who doesn't look after his health.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. But that's somebody who's ignoring a known risk to their health by continuing to smoke.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: It could be so and many of our patients have a passion for smoking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The reason I asked you earlier about how often you met with the Defence and what told you them is that they provide us with a summary of what you are going to testify to, which is based on their meetings with you. The summary we've received states that when Haradin Bala visited your clinic, it was approximately once every week during the time that you saw him.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Approximately. I don't know how many times exactly, but approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Harvey pointed out that it was about a seven-week period. Now, do you think you saw him seven times, ten times, or you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly whether it was seven, eight, or ten times, but I remember it was frequently. Every week he came once or even more times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, during -- let me ask you now about the 18th of July, 1998. I don't suppose you do, but do you remember where you were, what you were doing on that date?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The 18th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I don't remember, but considering the fact that I was in Shale most of the time, I must have been in Shale on this day because I didn't leave Shale during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember meeting a man named Ismail Berbatovci on or about that date?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You remember that name, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He was a journalist?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you don't recall meeting him at all when he came to Blinaje to try to interview Ram Buja on that date, 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No. I wasn't in Blinaje during this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You don't remember talking to him at all about coming back to complete the interview on a later date because Ram wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you know that on the 23rd of July, Ismail went -- had an appointment and went to meet Ram Buja. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you know that on about that date he disappeared and has never been seen again by his wife and children while he was on the way to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. interview Ram Buja?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No. I don't know about this case that you're mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You don't know about it at all? You don't know that he disappeared in July?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Let me explain, if possible. When the war ended, I heard that Ismail Berbatovci was on the list of missing persons, that is to say of persons who never returned back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You don't remember talking -- sending a message to his family on the 24th of July saying that he was being held by the KLA for questioning but he'd be released soon? Think hard.

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Never, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet his wife?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You never met her and told her he was taken by the KLA but there was nothing you could do?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I never spoke with her about this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you know he's on the list of missing persons. You also know he's never come off that list; he's still missing, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Well, I haven't seen him, considering the fact that he was an activist before the war as well and we carried out some activities together. But after the war, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you don't know that he was one of the people taken by the KLA in July 1998 who's never been seen again?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No, I don't know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was your pseudonym "Doctor" at this time? Did you have a pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you have a KLA pseudonym at this time?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a pseudonym, but people usually referred to me as a doctor, not as a pseudonym but as my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, based on your contacts with the KLA at that time with Shukri Buja and the other people you were working with, you know, don't you, in July 1998 the KLA was kidnapping and holding people prisoner?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I never knew about such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Just this, Doctor: You've just been asked a series of questions concerning violations, effectively, of the Geneva Conventions. Were you familiar with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I have read these conventions, especially the convention on war prisoners, the convention on the conduct towards civilians dating -- dating to 1949 and approved in 1950. I have known these conventions as a member and a director of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you provided any specific recommendations or regulations to be adopted by the KLA in respect of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. Not specifically linked with the Geneva Convention or some particular convention, but in relation to the health activity in the ranks of the KLA. I did that by December and I prepared rules in December 1998, which I submitted for approval to the General Staff then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Finally, you were asked about the physical examinations that you conducted of Haradin Bala. Were there any other physical manifestations of the face or any other part of the anatomy that confirmed your concern that he was genuinely suffering from a serious heart condition, any other matters that you haven't mentioned to far?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, they're almost done, but I don't think that's something that's proper. That's something you think would have been brought out on the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was distracted for a second. I can carry on? With the microphone on. I should do this more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor, were there any other physical manifestations?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: I remember from the frequent visits of Mr. Bala that based on all the symptoms, physical and clinical symptoms, I noted that he was suffering from some serious health condition. He showed manifestations because I didn't have other possibilities to confirm his symptoms, other than what I could with the means I had at my disposal. His lips were bluish. His general condition was such that he suffered from a heart condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What do bluish lips indicate?

utterances.speaker: FITIM SELIMI
utterances.text: The bluish lips are an indication of a phase where due to the constriction of the coronaries, the patient is going towards heart insufficiency. That is, the heart cannot supply with oxygenated blood, the periferic [as interpreted] nerves. This shows that he was at the initial phase of heart insufficiency. All the symptoms that I mentioned suggested to me this. This is why I told him to ask for more specialised assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you very much. That concludes the questions that are to be asked of you, so you may now return to your home and practice. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your next witness, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we might ask for the Chamber's indulgence. We have another witness who is on standby, but apparently is not in the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You think tomorrow at 2.15?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think tomorrow at 2.15 and we will have more than enough witnesses to fill the day. We have -- one witness apparently did not get on a plane but they will be here in due course, so we will be able to fill out the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I would suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are told a third witness has arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect. Well, then I would -- I would be more than happy to use the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's Mr. Bylykbashi, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be Skender Bylykbashi, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Where do you presently live, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I live in Bajice village, in Lipjan municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And how long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I have lived there for about 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you presently employed?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What do you do for a job, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I work at the post office, responsible for legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that you're responsible for legal affairs, what kind of legal affairs are you responsible for, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Related mostly to ownership. That is, I deal with complaints related to properties of the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I am a lawyer. I have graduated for law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say that you "have graduated for law," are you an individual who practices in a courtroom such as this or are your efforts in another area?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I am a lawyer by profession. I am a general lawyer or jurist. I deal with legal representation up to a certain level in the courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to ask you if you know Haradin Bala.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I first met him sometime in the middle of June or July. I am not certain about the day, in the year 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At the time that you met him in the middle of June or July in 1998, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I was in Bajice village, now as called Bajice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you meet him? How did that come about, if you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: At that time I was active in the organisation of the village because of the very difficult situation prevailing and Haradin had brought flour for his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "Haradin had brought flour for his family," what family had Haradin brought flour for?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: His narrow family, that is the family of the brother of his wife, who lives in the same village as me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you met him you said that there was some -- it was "a difficult situation." At that point in time, were you a part of any fighting group or organisation?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Not yet, but I was active in the organisation of the guards' shifts because we villagers organised ourselves. We wanted to observe the movements of the Serb military and police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you a member of the KLA during that period of time in June and July 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: No, because I didn't have a weapon, but I had already expressed my desire to become a member. But I was waiting for a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you did, in fact, become a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: That was during the day of the beginning of the great offensive against the Lapusnik gorge on the 26th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the offensive of July 26th, 1998, can you tell us, if you recall, about how many times you saw Haradin Bala in your village?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I may have seen him four or five times; I cannot be sure because I know I have seen him later as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you saw him later as well, when would that have been?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I have seen him after the offensive when we started to re-organise ourselves and ever since we were almost together because we served in the same point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the offensive of July 26th when you saw him, did you have an opportunity to take stock of how he looked in any fashion?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I could take stock of how he looked because I was, myself, surprised at the way he was holding his weapon. He looked older than the other members or the other people who wanted to become members.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you were surprised, why were you surprised?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Because he seemed rather pale, tired, he had shadows under his eyes. He had a pallid look, he seemed to have bad health.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever have any conversation with him concerning his health at all?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was the first or the second time that I met him, but I know when he brought the flour I wanted to know where he got the flour from and I asked him, Where did you get it, the flour, how could you bring it here? He told me that he was working in Luzhnice, he was staying in Luzhnice serving in the storage there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Why were you --

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: The warehouse there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Why were you interested in flour, sir?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Because at that time it was not easy for us to find food supplies because our territory was surrounded by enemy forces and our movements were very limited. That's why I was eager to know about anything which was unusual in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, during that period of time - and once again I'm referring to the period in June and July when you saw him in Bajice - could you tell us when you did see him for how long a period of time you saw him? Did you see him for a quick minute, spend time with him, days, hours, minutes, or even seconds?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Now, I think our conversation -- our meeting lasted as long as the conversation I referred to about last. I cannot tell you how many minutes it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from the conversation that you had with him, did you have a chance to see him in the village itself during the period of time after you spoke with him or before you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I think I told you to my recollection I have seen him four or five times, but during the other times we had talked with each other less. That was a time we spoke more, that I mentioned, but I've seen him on other occasions, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And on the other occasions when you saw him, I take it those were times when you did not speak with him but you saw him in your village. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Please wait there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Bylykbashi, I hope I've pronounced your name correctly, my name is Alex Whiting; I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case. You testified that you served with Haradin Bala at the same point after the 26th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: In the beginning it was at Bajice gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long were you serving at Bajice gorge?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: To my recollection, I served for two or three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Haradin Bala was there during those two or three weeks?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes, he was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you go after those two or three weeks?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: After those two or three weeks, we went down to the village. It was a very difficult situation after the offensive. And for two or three weeks, as I remember, we didn't expose ourselves. We stayed at two or three different positions and the co-villagers brought us food.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say you went down to the village, is that the village of Bajince?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes, the village of Bajince.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to be clear, I think you addressed this, but just to be clear, it's now known as Bajince but during the war it was known as Bajice?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Bajice it was during war and now it's Baiz, B-a-i-z.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So during the war it was Bajice or Bajince?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I didn't show any particular interest in that. We called it Bajice, some others might have called it Bajince. With us the problem is that in the village we call it as we call it, the municipalities called it as they thought was the correct way to call it, and the occupier had his own purpose in calling it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Now, when you went down to the village for two or three weeks, was -- and you said you stayed in different positions -- two or three different positions, was Haradin Bala still with you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: He was there throughout that time. I wasn't alone. In the beginning we were 12 or 13 as far as I remember. We stayed in small groups. Sometimes we stayed all together and sometimes we spread in to groups of four, five, or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And at the end of that period of two or three weeks, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Inside the village. We concentrated in village houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this still the village of Bajice?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm always referring to Bajince, as far as this period is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left Bajice?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Sometime after the new year. We spent the New Year's Eve in Bajince and then the entire group went to Zabel i Ulet or correction Zabel i Nalte.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Haradin Bala stay with you that entire time in in Bajince until you left new year's -- after New Year's Eve?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes, he stayed with us through the entire time. He was with us even after the New Year's Eve in Zabel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where is Zabel?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Zabel is a small place south of Komorane village, correction, east of Komorane village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Approximately how far east?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: I believe 2 kilometres far east, not further.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What were you doing in Zabel? Were you still with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: In the beginning, meaning right after the new year, I in fact was the leader of the group that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What were Haradin Bala's duties?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI
utterances.text: Haradin Bala's task was to observe from a guestroom with binoculars the movement of the enemy because there was the main road Peja-Prishtine, and his task was to observe the movements of the enemy and to see how many vehicles were moving in both directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps that would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must adjourn now because of the time, and we will continue tomorrow at 2.15. If you could return then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of June, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
